claims.text: A phosphate conversion coating suppresses the onset of corrosion-related degradation in Q235 steel.
Suppression occurs through formation of a protective oxide layer.
The initial reference material is untreated, pre-exposure Q235 steel.
The intervention is application of a phosphate conversion coating to the Q235 steel surface.
The proposed environments include high humidity and saline exposure at 25°C and 80°C.
The coating treatment forms a dense, adherent, phosphate-based oxide layer on Q235 steel.
The phosphate conversion coating reacts with the steel surface to form the protective layer.
The protective layer reduces the availability of reactive surface sites to corrosive agents.
Reduced availability of reactive sites slows the electrochemical reactions responsible for corrosion.
Phosphate-coated Q235 steel will have a significantly lower corrosion rate than untreated Q235 steel under identical conditions.
Coated specimens will show lower mass loss, lower corrosion current density, and less surface pitting than untreated specimens.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to high-humidity or saline environments at temperatures up to 80°C.
Extreme pH or mechanical abrasion may compromise the coating and invalidate the proposed protection.
Coating effectiveness may depend on coating composition and exposure duration.
The controlled study compares coated and untreated Q235 specimens in 5% NaCl saline fog at 25°C and 80°C for 500 hours.
Mass loss, corrosion current density, EIS response, and SEM surface morphology are proposed as corrosion measurements.
The hypothesis is falsified if coated specimens exhibit corrosion rates, current densities, or surface degradation comparable to or worse than untreated controls.
